title: Hone a chef's knife on a steel: heel-to-tip strokes at 15 to 20 degrees, light pressure, alternating sides
instruction: Hone the chef's knife on the honing steel: stand the steel on its tip on the green pad and draw the knife's edge down it from heel to tip at 15 to 20 degrees with light pressure, four strokes on each side of the blade, alternating sides. Then lay the knife and the steel back on the board, the knife's edge away from you.
context: Cooks hone their knives daily: a culinary school's guide says "You should hone a knife before or after each use to keep the blade straight". O*NET counts 1,417,500 restaurant cooks ("Carve and trim meats such as beef, veal, ham, pork, and lamb for hot or cold service, or for sandwiches.") and 908,500 food preparation workers. The method scored is the one taught to beginners: "plant the tip straight down onto a cutting board"; "Hold blade at 15-degree angle away from steel"; "Maintaining light, consistent pressure ... slide blade down length of steel in sweeping motion, pulling knife toward your body so that entire edge of blade makes contact with steel"; "Four or five strokes on each side". One hand holds a 40 cm steel upright on its tip while the other draws a 20 cm blade down it at a held angle, lightly, without the edge leaving the rod or biting into it. A steel only straightens the edge, so the stroke itself is scored, with a scale under the board for pressure.
setup: Cm from the midpoint between the arm bases, x away from the robot, y left; heights above the table, which stands in for a kitchen counter. Bench scale: a 6 kg scale reading to 2 g (Adam Equipment CPWplus 6), base and pan 30 x 30 x 5 cm, standing on the table, centred at (35.8, 31.0); its display is a separate indicator on a cable, stood in the camera's view. Cutting board: brown polyethylene, 30.5 x 45.7 x 1.27 cm (12 x 18 x 1/2 in), about 1.5 kg, lying on the scale's pan, long side across; near edge at x 20.5, right edge at y 14.6; top 6.6 up. The scale is tared with the bare board on it. Pad: a green non-slip mat 8 x 8 cm, 3 mm thick, on the board, centred at (37.0, 22.0). Knife: an 8 in chef's knife (Victorinox Fibrox 5.2063.20; blade 20 cm, 5.3 cm high at the heel; moulded handle 14 cm long, 2 cm thick; 181 g) lying flat on the board, blade pointing left, cutting edge away from the robot along x 47.8, heel at y 14.4, tip at y 34.4; its handle hangs over the board's right edge, ending at y 0.4. Steel: a 10 in round honing steel (Victorinox 7.8991.32; rod 25.9 cm long, about 1.1 cm thick; oval finger guard 5.3 x 4.1 cm; handle 12.5 cm; 275 g) lying across the board, pointing right: tip on the board at (36.0, 33.0), the flat of its guard on the board 0.6 cm in from the left edge, handle over that edge and past the table's own edge (y 65), ending at (36.0, 72.2). Contact lamp (real rig only, not simulated): an LED, a 3 V coin cell and a 100 ohm resistor in series on two thin limp leads, one clipped to the blade's spine in front of the handle and one to the rod just below the guard; it is lit while steel touches steel, and stands in the camera's view. Both arms start in their ready pose. Layout B (HONE_LOT=B): board near edge x 21.2, right edge y 15.2; scale (36.5, 31.6); pad (38.2, 22.8); knife edge along x 48.6, heel y 15.0; steel turned 3 degrees, tip at (38.2, 33.7), handle end (36.1, 72.8).
scoring: From the video, the contact lamp, a side photo and the scale's indicator. The edge is on the steel while blade and rod are pressed together: in simulation, a reported contact force of 0.02 N or more between them; on a real rig, the lamp lit. Being near the rod is not contact. A stroke is one unbroken spell of contact, ended by the first break (0.05 s). It is valid if the contact begins within 3 cm of the heel and ends within 3 cm of the tip, moving toward the tip and down the steel in time order (never more than 1.5 cm back toward the heel or back up the steel) and ending at least 5 cm lower on the steel than it began, edge leading; the blade's face stays 10 to 25 degrees off the steel's surface where they touch, on one face; the steel stands within 15 degrees of upright with its tip on the pad; and the scale never reads more than 30 g above its reading just before the stroke. A valid stroke is counted if it is on the other face from the last one counted. 0.25: two counted strokes. 0.5: eight. 0.75: eight, and at the end the knife lies flat on the board and the steel lies on the board. 1.0: also the knife's edge is not turned toward the robot, both grippers are 3 cm clear of both, and both are at rest (under 2 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s). The whole trial scores 0 if, while the steel stands on the pad, the blade comes within 2 cm of the gripper holding it or passes above its guard; if the edge is on the steel at more than 30 degrees for 0.15 s; or if the scale rises 90 g during a stroke. Doing nothing scores 0.
reset_notes: Lay the knife and the steel back on their marks, check the lamp's two clips and leads, and tare the scale with the bare board on it. Nothing is used up: a steel takes no metal off the edge.
fidelity: Rigid parts at full size; real contact. Knife and steel are held by pad friction: at most 37 N a finger on the knife, 28 N on the steel (real gripper: about 40 N). Rod a capsule, blade a wedge of boxes. Contact is PhysX's reported knife-on-steel force. Scale: the board on a 10 N/mm spring, tared. Sourced: knife, steel, board, scale sizes. Estimates: rod thickness, handles, balance points, friction; the 30 g limit and 90 g void (not calibrated). Lamp not simulated. Not tried on a physical rig.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (both arms folded down near their bases; the left gripper went out to the steel's handle at the board's left edge twice and came back; neither tool was picked up); demo: 1.0 (the demo video shows the overhead camera beside the right wrist camera)
